name: Nora Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government, and your answers stay confidential. What happens on a usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and have managed the payroll corrections team at a large construction company for six years. Eight people bring me missed overtime, wrong shift rates and deductions that do not match the contract. I have a bachelor’s degree and know the ordinary cases well, though I still need the legal adviser for a difficult dispute. I have never used an AI tool; I trust the signed timesheet and the worker who can explain it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband drives a delivery van, and our children are nine and fourteen. We have a mortgage, less than one month of expenses saved and lower pay than most managers here. There are few similar payroll jobs nearby. I know the work, but our bank account does not have room for even a short gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AI Plateau changes little. A routine email may be quicker, but someone still has to return the missing overtime to the worker’s pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I am already worried about the mortgage and the van’s repair bills. Less than a month saved means one bad week can make us late. A small tool may not fire anyone, but management might leave a clerk vacancy unfilled and give us the same work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep checking the signed timesheet before approving a correction and ask our staff representative whether the vacant clerk post is being filled. We would stop paying for a second streaming service and put the monthly amount by for van repairs. If a basic email tool arrives, I would ask another manager to show me its mistakes before I sign a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. The AI picture is mild, but our bills are not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which payment keeps you awake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage on the first of the month. When my husband’s van needed tyres last spring, we paid the mortgage but almost emptied the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask about the clerk vacancy now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clerk left in September and the team is carrying those timesheets. I want a date for a replacement, not praise for coping. If the answer is no, I would ask the representative to put the workload in writing.

say: **AI Plateau** may speed email, but workers still need missing overtime paid.
The team needs a **clerk replacement** for its current workload.
think: The **mortgage** and van repairs already make a bad week dangerous.
A vacant **clerk post** may stay empty while our workload remains.
do: **Check** signed timesheets before each correction in 2026.
**Ask** the staff representative for a clerk replacement date.
**Cancel** the second streaming service and save the fee for van repairs.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary bills despite mild AI change.
S0.quote: When my husband’s van needed tyres last spring, we paid the mortgage but almost emptied the fridge.
fieldNote: Her **thin cushion** keeps baseline worry high even when the technology itself changes little.
She asks a **staff representative** about a real vacancy rather than quietly accepting more timesheets.

steps.text: Check signed timesheets before approving payroll corrections
Ask staff representative for a clerk replacement date and workload record
Cancel second streaming service and keep fee for van repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write replies, check hours, book shifts and answer simple payroll questions. Workers need a clear right to challenge a wrong payslip before anyone counts staff savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office is exactly the kind of screen work that could shrink. I have six years as a manager, but my pay is low and the company might combine our team with another. My own post could be affected; with less than a month saved and few local openings, I cannot shrug that off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d take a folder of correction cases to the staff representative and ask for a written rule on human review. I would keep checking overtime against signed sheets, and if the company offers paid instruction on a new system I’d attend with a colleague. If my hours fall, we would stop the children’s paid sports club before putting the mortgage on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about what a cut would do to our household. I am steady at work because the team needs me, not because the money is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case goes into the folder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mason worked three late shifts, but one was coded as ordinary time. The payslip was neat and wrong. I called the site supervisor and got the signed sheet before we corrected it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why attend with a colleague?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not learn a new system by clicking through alone at night. If the company is changing payroll, it can pay two of us to check the work. I would ask my colleague to stop me when I miss a rule.

say: **Payroll automation** must leave workers a human review route.
I’d use **signed sheets** to challenge a tidy but wrong payslip.
think: Our screen-heavy office could **shrink or merge** with another team.
My post is at risk, and **thin savings** make even reduced hours serious.
do: **Bring** correction cases to the staff representative this month.
**Attend** paid system instruction with a colleague if offered.
**Pause** the children’s sports club if work hours fall.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a possible pay cut and an empty buffer.
S1.quote: The payslip was neat and wrong.
fieldNote: Her **experience** does not remove job risk when payroll checking can be automated.
She will attend **paid instruction** with a coworker, despite never having used AI before.
She says **alarmed**, while describing a possible cut to her own hours or post rather than an expected dismissal.

steps.text: Give signed correction cases to staff representative for human-review talks
Attend paid new-system instruction with a colleague if offered
Pause children sports club if payroll hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could check hours, write corrections and handle most payroll questions without us. I’d ask for a cut date and a guarantee that workers can appeal a machine’s pay decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI in 2028 could do almost all of our desk work. Robots able to do physical site work come around 2031, but my job does not wait for them. I expect our payroll team to be cut and my manager post may go too. My husband’s delivery wage alone cannot pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d ask the staff representative to demand notice and severance figures, then my husband and I would call our mortgage lender about temporary payment options before missing a bill. In 2027 I’d apply for the one advertised payroll manager job across the region only if its take-home pay after travel covers our house and children’s costs. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I am cut, I’d accept a real offer rather than wait for a perfect manager title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I have people to call. A few weeks of savings cannot carry a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether a short payment arrangement is possible and how much it costs later. I would not call it free money. My husband should hear the answer with me before we agree to anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on an advert. We would try the commute first if an actual offer came, and compare the travel bill with the wage. The children are in school here and we cannot pay two rents on a guess.

say: **AGI by 2028** needs cut figures and a human payroll appeal.
I’d ask for **written notice** before the team disappears.
think: Payroll thinking work could go in **2028**, before site robots around 2031.
My own post may go; one delivery wage cannot cover the **mortgage**.
do: **Request** notice and severance figures through the staff representative tomorrow.
**Call** the mortgage lender with my husband before missing a payment.
**Apply** for the regional job only if net pay covers bills; try commuting only after a real offer.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a short cushion and few local options.
S2.quote: A few weeks of savings cannot carry a long search.
fieldNote: Her **own job risk** meets a mortgage, few nearby vacancies and less than one month saved.
She treats a **lender arrangement** as a costed option, not new savings or free help.

steps.text: Ask staff representative to seek written notice and severance figures
Apply for regional payroll role only if net pay after travel covers family bills
Try regional commute only after a real offer and if pay after travel covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives the company time to tell us which payroll jobs remain. I would ask for a paid place in worker-pay appeals, with a real right to correct a wrong decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My payroll checking could still go in 2031, and appeal work also reads records and writes decisions, so it faces AGI then too. Robots doing hands-on site tasks arrive around 2034 and do not shelter either desk. Five years gives us time to pay down debt if wages hold, but I cannot count on a new post here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beginning in January 2027 I’d ask to handle one paid appeals case a month with the senior adviser checking my decision, if my manager allows time away from the payroll queue. I’d take the company’s appeals course only if it pays for it and keeps my salary. After 2031 I’d apply for an appeals manager post only if it is still advertised, can reverse a wrong pay decision and covers our mortgage after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. There is a little more room to learn, though the same computer could reach the appeals desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the adviser to correct?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I read the contract and the worker’s signed hours properly. I know ordinary overtime, but a disputed allowance can depend on a clause I have not used. I would write down the mistake rather than hide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is on unpaid evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take it. My husband is often on a late delivery route, and our younger child needs someone at home. I would ask for paid time or wait for a funded place.

say: **Five years** should bring paid appeal work with real correction powers.
An unpaid evening course is not a **usable route** for my family.
think: Payroll and appeals desk work both face **2031 AGI**.
If wages hold, I could pay down **debt** over five years, but I cannot count on a new appeal post.
do: **Handle** one paid appeal monthly from January 2027 if queue cover is approved.
**Take** appeals training only with company funding and full salary.
**Apply** after 2031 only for advertised appeals work with reversal authority and mortgage pay after travel.
feel: I feel **anxious** about another desk role, with time to test it.
S3.quote: I know ordinary overtime, but a disputed allowance can depend on a clause I have not used.
fieldNote: She is **experienced in overtime**, but identifies a gap in disputed allowances and contract clauses.
The **paid appeal trial** requires queue cover and childcare, while appeal paperwork remains exposed in 2031.

steps.text: Handle monthly paid appeal only with manager queue cover and senior-adviser review
Take appeals course only with company funding and full salary
Apply after 2031 for advertised appeals role only with reversal authority and mortgage pay after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 is enough notice to put worker pay rights in writing now. I’d ask the staff representative to seek a named human appeal and yearly figures on payroll errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 our children will be about nineteen and twenty-four, and we might have reduced the mortgage if both wages hold. My payroll and appeals screen work still faces AGI then; robots for physical site tasks arrive around 2039. Ten years does not make our thin savings feel rich today, but it gives me time to look for paid work with real authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep checking signed sheets and put a small amount into savings only after both wages and the mortgage clear. I’d ask the staff representative each year for written error and appeal figures. Before 2036 I’d take a paid worker-pay role if offered without a wage cut; after AGI arrives I’d stay only if it still lets me reverse wrong decisions and pays our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the bills we have now, though I can use ten years to prepare. I do not want the company to call an unpaid course a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twenty after a full month when my husband has all his delivery shifts. We would skip it if the van needs work. I would not put the transfer on automatic while the account is this thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep you in a worker-pay role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real wage and authority to correct the record when a worker has been underpaid. I would ask for that authority in the job description. A title without the power to fix the payslip would be a poor bargain.

say: A **decade** should bring a named human appeal and published payroll error figures.
I’d ask the staff representative for **yearly records**.
think: Both wages could reduce the **mortgage** by 2036 if they hold.
Payroll and appeals screens face **2036 AGI**, before site robots around 2039.
do: **Save** twenty only in full-pay months with my husband’s full shifts, mortgage paid, and no van repair.
**Take** a worker-pay role before 2036 only if offered without a wage cut.
**Stay** after 2036 only while the role reverses wrong pay decisions and covers household bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about present bills despite a longer preparation period.
S4.quote: A title without the power to fix the payslip would be a poor bargain.
fieldNote: Her **thin savings** and van costs still shape the 2026 budget under a ten-year scenario.
She wants **reversal power** and a real wage, not a title or unpaid course.

steps.text: Keep checking signed timesheets before payroll corrections
Save twenty only in full-pay months with husband’s full shifts, cleared mortgage, and no van repair
Ask staff representative yearly for payroll error and appeal figures
Take worker-pay offer without wage cut; stay after 2036 only with reversal authority and sufficient pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because this payroll team could go before I can find another wage near home. A cut date, severance in numbers and a real paid role that can fix wrong pay would help. I cannot meet a mortgage with a promise to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the mason whose late shift was coded at the ordinary rate whether the payslip looked accurate. A neat screen can still leave a worker short on rent. I want the signed sheet beside the number.

headlineQuote: A neat screen can still leave a worker short on rent.
portrait: **Nora, 43**, is an experienced payroll corrections manager at a large construction company with a bachelor’s degree.
Her **low pay**, under-one-month savings, mortgage, two children and few local jobs make even brief wage loss serious.
She has **never used AI** and checks signed timesheets with workers and supervisors before correcting pay.
She stays **anxious** in AI Plateau, is alarmed by rapid cuts and wants a paid human appeal role with real authority.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her payroll post before she finds another wage near home.
whatWouldHelp: A firm **cut date**, numeric severance and a paid role able to reverse wrong pay would help.
